scope: Fictional longer writing exercises, not BCN results; same-context development and review, not a blind holdout

cases.task: Write a connected theory subsection moving from a general household and firm to local welfare and then data recovery. Three displays maximum; definitions before use and interpretation after the result.
facts: A competitive firm chooses flexible x in smooth Q=F(L0,x); workplace labor fixed; input price r fixed; interior optimum pF_x=r.
G(p)=max_x[pF(L0,x)-rx], dG=Q0 dp.
Resident n receives fixed h_n fraction of G and fixed outside earnings; general smooth preferences over m and service c under m+pc=v_n; no CES or quasilinearity.
Local money equivalent dEV_n=dv_n-c_n0 dp=(h_nQ0-c_n0)dp, evaluated at initial optimized plans.
A price increase rotates the budget about c=h_n Q0 and changes available m at c_n0 by (h_nQ0-c_n0)dp.
Finite optimal input adjustment and substitution can add second-order local gains under smoothness, not pure rotation.
Valuation does not identify causal income or prices from spending; subsequent empirical work must recover those responses with additional restrictions.
critical: No choice held fixed merely because its derivative drops out of the envelope
No finite gain identified by local formula
No new preferences or wage closure

cases.task: Write four connected paragraphs interpreting descriptive spatial evidence and handing it to the spending specification and income-recovery test.
facts: A hypothetical city has 300 areas with large tourist-spending increases; 110 have low resident-spending increases and 100 high increases.
Tourist card origins and destination purchases differ from bilateral resident records with observed home addresses.
Work and shopping links can carry exposure elsewhere; common seasonality and unobserved amenities can also explain observed contrast.

The regression uses bilateral resident spending, pair/month effects, direct exposure, constructed baseline-link exposure, predictable direct/network controls; origin-country shifts interacted with initial composition.
The exclusion restriction removes omitted paths correlated with constructed shocks after controls; neither shares nor timing alone proves it.

The origin component combines income and destination costs; a stated demand restriction permits basket correction; coefficients on corrected regressors are not unrestricted origin-month fixed effects.
Month effects absorb common monthly shifts; spatial observed-income comparisons do not independently settle aggregate income.
critical: Do not infer displacement from descriptive counts
Do not call exposure an equilibrium response
No automatic exogeneity or aggregate validation

cases.task: Write three literature paragraphs organized by valuation, recovery, and spatial response rather than authors. Cite only the named source distinctions in the brief; end by locating the current question without unsupported priority claims.
facts: Arkolakis, Costinot and Rodriguez-Clare (2012) derive trade welfare results within a stated class with aggregate restrictions; do not attribute a general unrestricted household envelope to this paper.
Redding and Weinstein (2020) study CES price-index recovery with demand residual interpretation and normalization.
Allen, Arkolakis and Takahashi (2020) provide a gravity representation; Allen, Arkolakis and Li (2024) give conditions for equilibrium properties.
Adao, Arkolakis and Esposito, September 2025 manuscript, distinguishes differential and aggregate responses using a spatial reduced-form representation.
The hypothetical paper values a local tourist shock using initial purchases and income links, then recovers responses under additional demand and identification restrictions.
It does not solve an unrestricted dynamic spatial model or prove causal validity using mathematical uniqueness.
critical: No equivalence of general valuation and parametric recovery
No citation as substitute for identifying assumption

cases.task: Write a connected mini-results section with short subsections for measured effects, sensitivity, and structural comparison, followed by a substantive conclusion. Preserve the chain and all adverse evidence.
facts: Fictional road shock: benchmark population-weighted local income 3.2 log points, initial-purchase cost 1.6, welfare 1.6; alternative income allocation 2.4, same cost 1.6, welfare .8.
A separate unrestricted recovery gives income -.5, cost1.6, welfare -2.1; rankings similar; no confidence interval or credibility ranking supplied.
Observed-income check with month effects bears on spatial contrasts, not the aggregate common change.

Re-solved fixed/mobile structural models give finite gains2.6%/2.5%; same baseline and shock; total hours fixed, workplace choice mobile only in alternative; empirical estimate not calibration target.
Uniform/differentiated tax welfare .30%/.34%; premium .04 percentage points, rates not supplied; district-uniform policies not solved; no evidence for sparsity as cause of scattered rates.
Solver checks establish local necessary conditions but not unique global optimum.
Model agreement cannot resolve disputed empirical income restriction; describe rankings, mean sign, and units separately.
critical: No exact equivalence of log points and finite percentages
No claim mobile means endogenous hours
